definitions.definition: The beneficial object (artha) whose defining mark is Vedic injunction (codanā) — concretely the sacrifice and other enjoined acts, which join a person with the highest good; what is enjoined but harmful (e.g. the Śyena, whose aim is violence) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose, made known by the Veda (Arthasaṅgraha): the sacrifice and the like.
What is made known by prohibition as leading to harm (anartha), e.g. the violence aimed at in the Śyena rite; also the demerit (pāpa) that results.
The inquiry into dharma through the investigation of Vedic sentences, undertaken after Vedic study and before returning from the teacher's house (MS 1.1.1 with Śabara).

The statement that impels to action (Śabara); the injunction, which alone makes known dharma, including what is future, subtle or remote. Śabara on MS 2.1.5 also uses 'codanā' for the apūrva the injunction makes known.

equivalents.note: codanā is the older (sūtra/bhāṣya) word; vidhi is the manual term, which also names one of the five kinds of Vedic sentence

definitions.definition: The part of the Veda that makes known an unknown purposeful object; fourfold as originative, applicatory, performative and eligibility injunction (Arthasaṅgraha); also classed as apūrva, niyama and parisaṅkhyā injunctions.
An injunction conveys a command (niyoga), 'what is to be done' (kārya), which prompts the qualified person by itself.
An injunction that conveys only the form of the act, e.g. 'he offers the Agnihotra'.
An injunction that conveys the relation of subsidiary and principal, e.g. 'he offers with curd'; assisted by the six means (śruti etc.).
The principal injunction, united with the subsidiary injunctions, that conveys the prompt, uninterrupted performance of the whole rite in a fixed sequence.
An injunction that conveys ownership (enjoyership) of the fruit of the act, e.g. 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'.
An injunction of what is not obtained by any other means at all (e.g. sprinkling the rice).
An injunction that fixes one means where the end could be reached optionally by several (e.g. husking to remove the husk).

An injunction that, where something is obtained both in the stated case and elsewhere, serves to exclude the others (e.g. 'five five-nailed animals may be eaten'); explicit (śrautī) or implied (lākṣaṇikī).
A sentence that turns a person away from an act that brings harm; one of the five kinds of Vedic sentence.

A negation that does not attach to the injunctive but forms a positive injunction of 'not-doing' (e.g. the snātaka's vow not to look at the rising sun), used where a prohibition proper is impossible or would create an option.
The portion of the Veda recited during the rite as prompting its performance; the rest is Brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33). Mantras have meaning like ordinary sentences (MS 1.2.40).
Mantras are meaningful by reminding the performer of items connected with the performance; an unseen purpose for their recitation is assumed only where no seen purpose is possible.
Whatever in the Veda is not mantra (MS 2.1.33): the injunctions, arthavādas and the like.
A mantra whose division into feet depends on the sense (MS 2.1.35).
The name for what is sung (MS 2.1.36).
The name for the remaining mantras, neither metrically divided by sense nor sung (MS 2.1.37).
A word in an injunction that names the rite rather than enjoining a quality (e.g. udbhid, citrā, agnihotra, śyena) (MS 1.4.2–5).
Meaningful by delimiting what is enjoined; a word is taken as a name for four reasons — avoiding secondary meaning, avoiding a split sentence, another text supplying the quality, and comparison.

Vedic passages that do not themselves enjoin; they are meaningful as praise of what is enjoined, forming one sentence with the injunctions (MS 1.2.7). A fruit stated for a subsidiary is arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).

A sentence whose purport is praise or blame; supplementing an injunction or a prohibition; classified as praise, blame, another's deed and ancient narrative, or as figurative (guṇavāda), restating (anuvāda) and fact-stating (bhūtārthavāda).

An arthavāda that conflicts with another means of knowledge and is taken figuratively (e.g. 'the sacrificial post is the sun'; 'the sacrificer is the grass-bundle') (MS 1.2.10; grounds listed at MS 1.4.23–28).
An arthavāda stating what is already known by another means of knowledge (e.g. that fire is a remedy for cold).
An arthavāda neither contradicted nor already established by another means (e.g. 'Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vṛtra').
The function of arthavāda: praising the enjoined act so as to prompt a person held back by laziness (MS 1.2.7).
Arthavāda that blames what is prohibited (e.g. the story of Rudra's weeping, supplementing 'silver is not to be given on the barhis').
Arthavāda recounting a deed done by another great person.
Arthavāda narrating what was done or said in former times.
The authorless (apauruṣeya), beginningless body of sentences, the sole means of knowing dharma; it comprises injunction, mantra, name, prohibition and arthavāda.
The Veda, as distinct from smṛti; also, in the theory of application, direct statement (see trm:sruti-mimamsa).

The Veda's having no author, human or divine; names like Kāṭhaka come from expounding, not authorship (MS 1.1.30); the unbroken chain of teachers' study has no first term (ŚV vākya 366); since defects of testimony depend on speakers, an authorless Veda is free of them (ŚV codanā 62).
The teaching or recitation of a Vedic recension by a master, from which its name (e.g. Kāṭhaka) derives (MS 1.1.30).
In MS 1.1.5, the (Vedic) instruction that is the means of knowing dharma.
Texts of human authors learned in the Veda; authoritative because a Vedic source can be inferred from them, but disregarded where they conflict with the Veda or show a worldly motive (MS 1.3.1–4).
Practices of the learned (śiṣṭa) done with no visible motive, accepted as indicating Vedic injunctions (MS 1.3.7).
The highest good with which what injunction makes known joins a person (Śabara on MS 1.1.2); for Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara, the fruit of dharma done as an offering to Govinda/Īśvara.
The unseen potency brought about by a perishable ritual act, postulated because the fruit (e.g. heaven) comes later: 'there is an apūrva, since the undertaking is enjoined' (Śabara on MS 2.1.5).
A capacity produced in the self (or the act) by the rite; later Bhāṭṭas distinguish the final apūrva of the fruit from those of the parts and subsidiaries.
The apūrva is the 'what is to be done' (kārya/niyoga) made known by the injunction itself, knowable only from the Veda.

equivalents.note: Both name the unseen result of acts that ripens later; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika places adṛṣṭa in the self and makes Īśvara its overseer, which Mīmāṃsā rejects

notes: The Bhāṭṭa subdivision of apūrvas (e.g. phala-, samudāya-, utpatti-, aṅga-apūrva) is from memory (low); not attached to a teaching.

definitions.definition: Unseen force; used by Śāstradīpikā for what awakens impressions in dreams, and generally for the unseen results of acts, of which apūrva is the Mīmāṃsā form.

The operation of the one who brings about, expressed by the verbal suffix: verbal (śābdī) bhāvanā — the prompting power of the injunctive — and objective (ārthī) bhāvanā — the person's activity toward the result; each expects what (sādhya), by what (karaṇa) and how (itikartavyatā).
The prompter's operation conducive to a person's engaging in action, expressed by the injunctive (liṅ) element; in the Veda it resides in the word itself.
The activity toward an act produced by the desire for a purpose, expressed by the verbal ending as such: 'one should bring about heaven by the sacrifice in this way'.
The procedure — the subsidiaries (e.g. the prayājas) — that answers the question 'how?' of the bhāvanā; in an ectype it is taken from the archetype (MS 7.4.1).
The means (e.g. the sacrifice) answering the question 'by what?' of the bhāvanā.
The meaning of Vedic sentences and of the injunction: the act as what is to be done, known only from the Veda; all words mean in connection with it (kāryānvitābhidhāna).

equivalents.note: Prābhākaras use kārya (the to-be-done) and niyoga (the command) for the injunction's content from two sides

definitions.definition: The command conveyed by the injunctive, which by itself prompts the qualified person, independent of his desire for the fruit.

literal: being a means to the desired

definitions.definition: Maṇḍana Miśra's account of what the injunctive form conveys: that the act is a means to what the agent desires.

notes: Assigned to lin:bhatta-mimamsa because Maṇḍana is placed there by tradition; the view differs from Kumārila's.

definitions.definition: Acts enjoined for life (e.g. the Agnihotra 'as long as one lives'); performing them destroys earlier sin and averts the demerit of omission (Tantravārttika), and the seeker of release must perform them (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110).
Performed because enjoined; the command itself, not a fruit, is what prompts the performer (Prābhākara view as generally reported).
Acts enjoined on an occasion (e.g. the birth of a son, an eclipse); for the seeker of release they are to be performed like the obligatory ones.
Acts enjoined for one who desires a particular fruit (e.g. heaven, cattle); the seeker of release abstains from them because they produce further bodies.
Acts forbidden by the Veda, whose performance produces demerit; the seeker of release avoids them.
Rites enjoined on the occasion of a fault or failure in performance; treated in Mīmāṃsā as occasional acts (e.g. MS 6.4).
The demerit incurred by omitting enjoined (obligatory, occasional) acts; the seeker of release performs them to avoid it (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110; Tantravārttika).
Performing dharma with the thought of offering it to Īśvara (Laugākṣi Bhāskara) or Śrī Govinda (Āpadeva), which makes it a cause of the highest good.

The qualification of the agent entitled to perform a rite and enjoy its fruit: a human (MS 6.1.4–5), man or woman — husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17) — of the three higher varṇas, with Vedic learning (MS 6.1.25–38); the subject of adhyāya 6.
The eligible agent of a rite, the one to whom the fruit belongs ('one desiring heaven').
That which exists for the sake of another (MS 3.1.2); for Bādari only substances, qualities and purificatory acts, for Jaimini also acts (MS 3.1.3–4). Its correlate is the principal (śeṣin).
That for whose sake a subsidiary exists.
A subsidiary element of a principal rite (pradhāna), e.g. the prayājas of the new- and full-moon rites.
The principal act, which bears the fruit; its subsidiaries serve it (MS 9.1.1).
A subsidiary enjoined with reference to a material of the rite (e.g. husking, sprinkling), helping by acting on it.
A subsidiary enjoined by itself, not with reference to a material (e.g. the prayājas), helping only toward the final apūrva.
The first and strongest of the six means of determining subsidiarity: an independent word (case-ending, expression or single word) that directly states the relation (MS 3.3.14; Arthasaṅgraha).
The second means of determining subsidiarity: the capacity of a word or mantra to express something, which applies the mantra to it (MS 3.3.14).
A sentence is one when it has a single purpose and its parts need each other (MS 2.1.46); as the third means of subsidiarity, joint utterance (samabhivyāhāra) of subsidiary and principal words.

The fourth means of subsidiarity: mutual expectancy between a principal needing a procedure and subsidiaries without a stated fruit; major (of the main rite) and minor (of a subsidiary) (MS 3.3.14; Arthasaṅgraha).
The fifth means of subsidiarity: sameness of place in the text or in performance; also a means of fixing sequence (MS 3.3.14).
The sixth and weakest means of subsidiarity: a derived name, Vedic or worldly, such as 'the Hotṛ's cup' or 'ādhvaryava' (MS 3.3.14).

literal: for the sake of the rite

definitions.definition: What is done for the rite rather than for the person, as opposed to puruṣārtha (MS 4.1.1).

literal: for the sake of the person

definitions.definition: That which gives delight to a person, the desire for it being inseparable from it (MS 4.1.2); acts done for it are for the person, not for the rite.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from the 'four aims of life' sense of puruṣārtha.

definitions.definition: A rite whose subsidiaries are all taught in its own context (e.g. the new- and full-moon rites) is an archetype; one that lacks them and takes them by transfer is an ectype.
The extension of the procedure of an archetype to an ectype ('the ectype is to be performed like the archetype'), in general (adhyāya 7) and in particular (adhyāya 8).
Adapting transferred mantras, chants and purificatory acts to the ectype, e.g. replacing 'to Agni' by 'to Sūrya' (adhyāya 9).
The lapse of transferred details that serve no purpose in the ectype, e.g. husking for gold pieces (MS 10.1.1–2).
Performing a subsidiary once so that it serves several principal rites together, e.g. the prayājas for the several main offerings (adhyāya 11).

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from 'tantra' as a class of scripture.

definitions.definition: A subsidiary performed for one principal also incidentally benefiting another, e.g. the animal's prayājas benefiting the animal-cake (adhyāya 12).
The order of performance, fixed by direct statement, purpose, textual order, position, the order of principals and the order once begun (MS 5.1.1; Arthasaṅgraha).
A different verb, which marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.1); first of the six means of distinguishing rites.
Repetition of an injunction, which would be pointless unless it marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.2); in Vedānta usage one of the six marks of purport.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from abhyāsa 'practice' in Yoga.

definitions.definition: Being one sentence with another, by which arthavādas and subsidiary statements share the purport of an injunction (MS 1.2.7, 2.1.46).
Taking one utterance as several sentences, a fault to be avoided in interpretation (MS 2.1.47; Śabara on 1.1.1).
The mutual need of the parts of a sentence, which makes them one sentence (MS 2.1.46).
The remainder of the passage, which settles a doubtful meaning (MS 1.4.29).
The result of a rite. A fruit stated for a subsidiary is praise (MS 4.3.1); where none is stated, heaven is the fruit (MS 4.3.15); for a principal rite the stated fruit is real (Ātreya, MS 4.3.18).
The unit of Mīmāṃsā discussion, with five members: subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view and conclusion (Nyāyamālā).
The Vedic passage under discussion in an adhikaraṇa.
The doubt about the passage that gives rise to an adhikaraṇa (also called sandeha, viśaya).
The relevance of a topic to the whole śāstra, the chapter and the quarter in which it stands.
The first, provisional answer to the doubt, stated in its strongest form before being set aside.
The final answer of an adhikaraṇa, reached after the prima facie view.
An interpretive principle established in an adhikaraṇa and applied elsewhere (e.g. the viśvajit maxim that heaven is the fruit where none is stated).

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense ('maxim'); distinct from Nyāya as a school.

definitions.definition: The intended sense of a passage, settled by the rules of interpretation; the determinants listed in Vedānta manuals as six marks (upakrama–upasaṃhāra, abhyāsa, apūrvatā, phala, arthavāda, upapatti) draw on Mīmāṃsā rules.
The beginning of a passage; its relative strength against the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) is argued by Appayya Dīkṣita in the Upakramaparākrama.
A cognition that apprehends what was not apprehended before and is free from defects in its causes and from contradicting cognition (Śāstradīpikā); six in number.
Every experience (anubhūti), as distinct from memory; five in number (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
The validity of a cognition, which arises and is known from the cognition itself; invalidity comes from outside.

All means of knowledge are valid of themselves, since a capacity not present in a thing cannot be given by another (ŚV codanā 47); invalidity is established only by a cognition that the object is otherwise or by knowledge of a defect in the cause (ŚV codanā 53). The Veda, having no author, has no source of defect.
Validity is intrinsic but is grasped by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the first cognition (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).
A later cognition that the object is otherwise, which (with knowledge of a causal defect) alone sets aside a cognition's validity.
A defect in the conditions producing a cognition (e.g. in the sense organ, or in a human speaker), knowledge of which sets aside its validity.
The novelty required of a means of knowledge: it apprehends what was not apprehended before (Śāstradīpikā).
Cognition other than memory; every experience is a means of knowledge (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Cognition arising in a person when the senses are in contact with an existing object; it grasps only what is present and so cannot know dharma (MS 1.1.4).
First an indeterminate bare awareness, then determinate cognition by universal and other features; both are perception (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
Cognition of an unperceived part from seeing another part whose relation is known; of two kinds, by a relation seen directly or by one seen in general (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Cognition of an unperceived object from words (śāstra); the Vedic word is independently valid; a human word only when the speaker is reliable and the matter within reach of other means.
Similarity producing knowledge of an unperceived object: seeing a gavaya one cognizes the similarity in the remembered cow (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would not be possible (Devadatta, alive and not at home, is outside) — the Vṛttikāra in Śabara; accepted by both Bhāṭṭas and Prābhākaras.
Where the five positive means of knowledge do not arise, the non-apprehension itself is the means of knowing non-existence (ŚV abhāva 1; the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Not a separate means: the Prakaraṇapañcikā counts five means only; absence is grasped as the bare locus (as the Kāśikā on the Ślokavārttika reports the Prābhākara view).
Another name for the sixth means of knowledge, by which absence is known.
The first bare awareness of an object, like an infant's or a mute's, born of the pure object (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
The perception that follows the bare awareness and grasps the thing with its universal and other properties; also perception.
The initial non-conceptual awareness (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
A property produced in the object by cognition (its being manifest, prākaṭya), from which the cognition — itself not perceived — is inferred (Śāstradīpikā).

equivalents.note: two Bhāṭṭa names for the same property

definitions.definition: The manifestness of an object produced by cognition; another name for jñātatā.
The triad of knower, known and knowing, all manifested by every cognition, which is self-luminous (tripuṭī-pratyakṣa).
Cognition (saṃvid) manifests itself without another cognition; the self and the object are manifested by it.
The reflective cognition 'I know this' that follows a cognition; for Murāri Miśra it grasps the first cognition's validity (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).
Theory of what appears in erroneous cognition; the Mīmāṃsā schools hold akhyāti (Prābhākara) and viparītakhyāti (Bhāṭṭa).
Error is not the appearance of an unreal object but the non-apprehension of the difference between a perception ('this') and a memory ('silver'); ignorance itself is non-apprehension.
The non-apprehension of the difference between the two cognitions that makes up error.
In error a memory appears without its 'that' character, as if it were a present experience.
Error apprehends a thing as other than it is: the related items are real, only the relation that appears is unreal (Śāstradīpikā).
The relation of word and meaning, not created by any person (MS 1.1.5); known from the beginningless usage of elders (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
The beginningless usage of elders, observing which children learn the meanings of words (as connected with action).
Words are eternal; utterance only manifests them, and a word is recognized as the same in every utterance (MS 1.1.18–23).
The eternal letters are the word: 'gauḥ' is g, au and ḥ (Upavarṣa); meaning is conveyed by the letters through their impressions, without a sphoṭa.
The audible noise (nāda) produced by effort, which manifests the eternal letters; its loudness increases, not the word (MS 1.1.17).

The grammarians' unitary word-entity distinct from the letters; rejected by Kumārila as superfluous, the letters themselves conveying meaning (ŚV sphoṭavāda); Upavarṣa already identified the word with the letters.
The universal, which is what a word means, because Vedic action is directed to it (MS 1.3.33).
The real universal; in MS 6.1.8 the class (human) as the eligible agent.
The meaning of a word; the word-meanings, once conveyed, convey the sentence-meaning (Śabara on MS 1.1.25). Also 'category' in ontology (Bhāṭṭas five, Prābhākaras eight).
The meaning of the whole sentence, conveyed by the word-meanings (Bhāṭṭa) or by words expressing meanings already connected (Prābhākara).

Words first express their own meanings and cease; the expressed meanings then connect to yield the sentence-meaning, as the flame is an intermediate stage in cooking with wood (Śabara on MS 1.1.25; ŚV vākya 342–343).
Words express their meanings only as already connected with other meanings, ultimately with what is to be done (kārya), as learned from elders' usage.
Indication of a related meaning; for the Bhāṭṭas the sentence-meaning is always 'indicated' by the word-meanings (as the Prakaraṇapañcikā reports their saying), and arthavādas indicate praise.
The self, distinct from body and cognition, known to itself, shown by desire, memory and recognition; taught by negation ('not this, not this') (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; manifested as the subject in cognitions of objects (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Eternal, the agent and enjoyer who reaps the fruits of rites in another world; known through reasoning and made firm by the Upaniṣads (ŚV ātmavāda 148).

Absolute dissolution of the threefold bond (body, senses, objects), when dharma and adharma are exhausted and no new body arises; not an enjoyment of pleasure (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 105–108; Śāstradīpikā).
The absolute ending of embodiment caused by the complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma; the self remains in mere being, without cognition or bliss (Prakaraṇapañcikā).

equivalents.note: Pārthasārathi's 'cutting off of all specific qualities of the self' parallels the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika apavarga; Mīmāṃsā grounds it in the exhaustion of ritual karma

definitions.definition: The final ending of embodiment that is release (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
The self's threefold connection with the world: the body (seat of experience), the senses (its instruments) and the objects (what is experienced) (Śāstradīpikā).
The body, as the locus in which the self experiences pleasure and pain.

The fruit of rites for 'one desiring heaven'; where no fruit is stated, heaven is understood (MS 4.3.15). Śabara concludes that the word denotes happiness (prīti) itself (on MS 6.1.1–2); a later cited verse describes it as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not followed by loss, brought by longing.
Happiness; what the word 'svarga' denotes (Śabara on MS 6.1.2); what is for the person is that which gives delight (MS 4.1.2).

That to which an offering is directed as named in the injunction or mantra; subordinate to the sacrificial act, which alone produces the fruit (MS 9.1.9); not established as embodied or eating the offering (Śabara).
Embodiment of the deity, which Śabara holds is not established: statements implying it are mantras and arthavādas not meant to assert it (on MS 9.1.9).
The principal enjoined act, the giving up of a substance with reference to a deity; it is what produces the apūrva and fruit (MS 9.1.1, 9.1.9).

notes: The definition 'giving up a substance with reference to a deity' is the standard manual formula, from memory (moderate).

definitions.definition: Rejected as director of dharma and adharma and as creator: the fruit comes from dharma and adharma with place, time and circumstance (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116); later Bhāṭṭas (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara) teach offering dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
A dissolution destroying everything, for which there is no means of knowledge; creation and dissolution are to be understood 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 68, 113).

One claimed to know everything, including dharma, directly; not established by perception, scripture or tradition; an omniscient by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but none knows dharma by perception (ŚV codanā 110–136).
Learning the Veda from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; every such study presupposes a teacher's study, without first beginning (ŚV vākya 366).
The Veda of one's own branch; the injunction to study it is the starting point of Mīmāṃsā in the Prābhākara account.
Denial of the Veda's authority and of the self and afterlife; Kumārila's effort is to lead Mīmāṃsā away from a Lokāyata reading onto the āstika path (ŚV pratijñā 10, ātmavāda 148).
Kumārila's description of the state of Mīmāṃsā before him: 'mostly made into Lokāyata' (ŚV pratijñā 10); the Nyāyaratnākara names Bhartṛmitra and others.
Violence is prohibited; hence the Śyena rite, whose aim is violence, is harmful (anartha) though the Veda states it as a means for one who wishes to harm (Śabara on MS 1.1.2).
Investigation of the meaning of the Veda; the school founded on Jaimini's sūtras (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā), distinguished from the Uttara Mīmāṃsā (Vedānta).
The earlier commentator whose exposition of MS 1.1.3–5 Śabara reproduces.
A regional custom discussed as an example of practices of some that are dharma for all (MS 1.3.15–23, per commentaries).
Where no fruit is stated for an enjoined rite, heaven is understood as its fruit (MS 4.3.15); used widely, e.g. by the Prakaraṇapañcikā.
